opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I think there are really two reasons, and they're related.

The first is that for most of the history of linguistics and cognitive science, we've had exactly one kind of system that could use language in a flexible, open-ended way, and that's people. That makes it very hard to ask certain questions, because you can't easily intervene on a human brain, you can't rerun someone's childhood with different input, and you can't look at every connection. Language models are, for the first time, a second example of a system that does something at least superficially similar to what we do with language. Whatever they're doing, they're doing it in a way we can poke at, perturb, retrain, and inspect at a level of detail that's impossible with humans. Even if they turn out to work very differently from us, having a contrast case is enormously valuable scientifically.

The second reason is that they're a kind of existence proof for some long-running debates. People argued for decades about what you can and can't learn just from exposure to text: whether you can get syntax, whether you can get anything like meaning, whether you need grounding in perception or action, whether you need built-in structure. These were mostly arguments from intuition. Now we have systems trained on an enormous amount of text with relatively weak built-in assumptions, and we can actually go look at what they've learned. Do they represent the world described in a document? Do they track the beliefs and goals of the person who wrote it? Do they build something like compositional structure? Some of the answers have been surprising, in both directions.

And I'd add that there's a scientific question about the models themselves, independent of what they tell us about people. We've built artifacts whose behavior we don't fully understand, and which we didn't really design in any detailed sense. Figuring out what's going on inside them, what kinds of representations and algorithms emerge from this training process, is a genuinely new kind of empirical science. In some ways it feels closer to biology than to traditional computer science: you have this complicated thing that came out of an optimization process, and you have to develop the tools and theories to explain it after the fact.

So even if nobody ever used these models for anything practical, I'd still think they were one of the most interesting objects to study right now.

r001.rationale: The response asks what language models learn from text, including whether they represent the described world and develop compositional structure, and connects this to their training data and assumptions.

r002.rationale: It separates using models as evidence about what can be learned from text from studying their internal representations and algorithms as a scientific subject in their own right, independently of what they reveal about people.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the honest answer is that language models are the first artifacts we've ever built that produce something that looks a lot like human language, at scale, without us having written down the rules. And that makes them interesting as objects of study almost regardless of whether they're useful for anything.

For most of the history of linguistics and cognitive science, the central question has been: what does it take to acquire and use a language? What kind of representations, what kind of learning mechanism, what kind of data? And those have been hard questions to answer empirically because you can't run controlled experiments on children, and you can't look inside a human brain at the level of detail you'd want. Now we have systems where we control the training data completely, we can read off every parameter, we can intervene on internal states, and they nonetheless end up with something that, at least on the surface, has a lot of the structure of human linguistic competence. So they're a kind of model organism. Not a perfect one, and I want to be careful about the analogy, but a place where you can actually ask questions like "does learning from text alone give you a representation of syntax?" or "what does a model know about the world after only seeing descriptions of it?" and get real answers.

The second thing is that they're an interesting case study in what emerges from a very simple objective. Next-token prediction is about as dumb a training signal as you could pick, and yet to do it well you end up having to build internal models of all sorts of things: who's speaking, what they believe, what the state of some described situation is. One line of work I've been involved in looks at whether, when you train a model on, say, descriptions of a board game or a simple environment, it ends up with an internal representation of the board state even though it never saw the board. And the answer is often yes, in a partial and messy way. That tells you something about the relationship between language and the things language is about, which is a question philosophers and linguists have been arguing about for a long time.

And the third piece, which is maybe the one I find most compelling, is that these models fail in very informative ways. When they get something wrong, the pattern of errors is data. Humans and models that both succeed at a task don't tell you much about mechanism, but if the model generalizes differently than people do, that's a clue about what people are doing that the model isn't, or vice versa. So I think even if the technology stagnated tomorrow, we'd have a decade of science to do just trying to understand what these things learned and why.

r001.rationale: The response presents as a scientific question whether training on descriptions alone can give a model an internal representation of a board state, and says this often happens in a partial way.

r002.rationale: It distinguishes language models as controllable systems for studying what learning from data produces from direct study of people, describing them as an imperfect “model organism” and noting the limits of experiments on children and access to the brain.

astra-6.text:
I think they give us a way to ask some very old questions about language and learning in a much more concrete way. How much can you learn about the world just from the things people say? What kinds of structure can you discover without somebody explicitly telling you the rules? Language models are interesting because you can give a learning system a relatively simple objective—predict what comes next—and get behavior that seems to require quite a lot of linguistic knowledge.

And then the scientific question is: what exactly has it learned? Is it using the same kinds of abstractions that we use? Where does that apparent understanding break down? You don’t have to think these models are faithful models of human cognition to find those questions interesting. They give us systems we can intervene on, change the training data for, and inspect in ways that are much harder with people. That creates an opportunity to test ideas about what learning from language can and can’t accomplish.

r001.rationale: It frames as scientific questions how much a next-token learner can learn from people’s language and what structure it can discover without explicit rules, and notes that changing training data can test those limits.

r002.rationale: It says the models need not faithfully model human cognition to be scientifically useful, distinguishing study of learning systems from direct study of human cognition.

sol-6.1.text:
I think they give us a new way to ask some very old questions about language and learning. How much can you learn about the world just by observing what people say? What kinds of structure can you acquire without anyone explicitly telling you what that structure is? And how does the way you learn affect the representations you end up with?

Language models are interesting because we can study those questions in a system that we can actually manipulate. We can change the training data, change the learning objective, and look at how the resulting behavior changes. That doesn’t mean we should assume they learn language the way humans do. But understanding where they succeed, where they fail, and where they arrive at similar behavior through different mechanisms can help us make those questions much more precise.

r001.rationale: The response asks what models can learn from observed language and what structure they acquire without explicit instruction, then points to changing the training data and objective to study those outcomes.

r002.rationale: It says we should not assume models learn language the way humans do and notes that similar behavior can arise through different mechanisms, distinguishing model study from direct claims about human learning.
